intro: Section 29.2 covers palliative care for psychiatry residents: how common anxiety, depression and delirium are in advanced disease and how to treat them (including the Endicott substitution criteria), disease-specific stresses, the patient-family unit and where people die, physicians' own reactions to dying patients, breaking bad news, truth-telling and informed consent, terminal care decisions, the persistent vegetative state versus brain death, the Quinlan case, advance directives (living will, health care proxy, DNR and DNI orders), caring for the family and dying at home, palliative care and pain (types of pain and the opioid table), other end-of-life symptoms, hospice, end-of-life care for newborns and children, and spiritual issues and alternative medicine. Law and programs described are mainly from the United States. Update boxes add current opioid conversion guidance, the dronabinol label, Medicare hospice rules, POLST, a date correction, and Philippine law on advance directives, death and palliative care.
objectives: Recognize anxiety, depression (using the Endicott substitution criteria) and delirium in patients with advanced disease, and outline their treatment.
Describe how to break bad news, balance truth-telling with hope, and obtain informed consent.
Tell the persistent vegetative state from brain death and explain what the Quinlan case established.
Compare the living will, health care proxy and DNR or DNI orders, and state what the Patient Self-Determination Act requires.
Classify pain as somatic, visceral, neuropathic or psychogenic, and apply the principles of opioid and adjuvant treatment.
Manage common end-of-life symptoms, explain hospice eligibility, and adapt care for dying children and for spiritual needs.
